uhud-shura.title: After Uhud: gentleness with those who erred, not reproach
participants: The Companions (especially the archers who left their positions)
uhud-shura.eventDescription: After some Companions made a group mistake that led to a setback at the Battle of Uhud, by disobeying the Prophet's ﷺ order to stay at their posts, he did not meet them with harsh rebuke. He kept treating them gently and kept consulting them, and a verse was revealed describing this character and commanding him to continue consulting them despite what had happened.
uhud-shura.historicalContext: The Battle of Uhud took place in the third year after the migration, and the verse was revealed afterwards in the context of its lessons.
uhud-shura.problemType: Dealing with a group mistake that led to major negative consequences
uhud-shura.responseType: Forgiving them, seeking forgiveness for them, and continuing to consult them instead of excluding them
emotionsAddressed: Anger at a group mistake that cost everyone dearly
The urge to exclude those who erred from one's circle of trust
principles: Gentleness after a group mistake keeps the team or community together
Continuing to consult those who erred is a message of trust that rebuilds the relationship
Harshness after a mistake may break apart those around you instead of reforming them
modernApplications: If your team made a mistake that cost you, start with forgiveness before detailed accountability
Keep involving those who erred in future decisions if the mistake was an honest misjudgement, not deliberate; this rebuilds trust
Avoid excessive harshness after crises; it usually drives people away rather than reforming them
notToApplyTo: This does not apply to deliberate mistakes or outright betrayal, but to errors of judgement or the result of impulsiveness
behaviorObservations: He did not exclude those who erred from later consultation
He kept treating them gently despite the size of the loss
The Quran asked him to seek forgiveness for them, not to reproach them
whatToAvoid: Treating every strategic mistake as betrayal deserving permanent exclusion
uhud-shura.reflection: Leadership that can bear the mistakes of those it leads without losing its standing is what builds real loyalty, not temporary fear.
keywords: my team made a big mistake
we lost because of a group mistake
should i fire the person who made a mistake
a work mistake cost the company a lot
my team messed up and it cost us

quranRefs.context: Revealed after the Battle of Uhud and the mistake some Companions made in disobeying the Prophet's ﷺ order
quranRefs.relevance: It links gentleness in dealing with a group mistake to continued trust through consultation

zayd-ibn-sana.title: Zayd ibn Sa‘nah: when suspicion turns into certainty of truthfulness
participants: ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him)
zayd-ibn-sana.eventDescription: Zayd ibn Sa‘nah, one of the senior Jewish rabbis, was owed a debt by the Prophet ﷺ. He came to him days before it was due, grabbed his garment and cloak very roughly and demanded his right in harsh words. ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab was about to answer him severely, but the Prophet ﷺ stopped him and told him to repay the debt well, and even to add to it for having frightened him. Zayd was moved by this forbearance, which — by his own account — he had been deliberately testing to see if it matched a prophetic quality described in his books, and he embraced Islam.
zayd-ibn-sana.historicalContext: This story is narrated among the accounts of scholars from the People of the Book who embraced Islam, and it shows the effect of the Prophet's ﷺ character in relationships built on trust.
zayd-ibn-sana.problemType: Facing bad manners or rudeness from someone you have financial dealings with or who has a right over you
zayd-ibn-sana.responseType: Forbearance despite the right to respond, and stopping others from escalating
emotionsAddressed: Anger at a rude demand for something genuinely owed
The urge to discipline someone ill-mannered even if their claim is valid
principles: Giving the other person their right does not stop their way of claiming it from being bad
Forbearance in sensitive financial situations can have a deeper effect than merely paying what is due
Stopping others from escalating on your behalf is part of controlling the situation
modernApplications: If someone rudely demands something you genuinely owe, separate their right to claim from their improper manner
Do not let a rude demand stop you from paying the right in full, and perhaps more than required
Stop those around you from adding to the tension in a situation that can be resolved calmly
behaviorObservations: He stopped ‘Umar from answering rudeness with the same
He ordered the debt to be paid with extra compensation for the fright, not merely settled
His character did not change even though the situation was a deliberate test by the other party
whatToAvoid: Confusing forbearance with bad manners with laxity in paying or claiming rights
zayd-ibn-sana.reflection: Sometimes a calm character in the hardest financial situations is the strongest message that can be given without words.
keywords: someone is owed something but asked rudely

hadithRefs.narrator: ‘Abdullah ibn Salam (may Allah be pleased with him), from Zayd ibn Sa‘nah

hatib-baltaa.title: Hatib ibn Abi Balta‘ah: verifying before judging one who broke trust
participants: Hatib ibn Abi Balta‘ah (may Allah be pleased with him)
‘Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him)
‘Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him)
hatib-baltaa.eventDescription: When the Prophet ﷺ secretly resolved to march on Makkah, Hatib ibn Abi Balta‘ah — a senior Companion who had fought at Badr — wrote a letter to Quraysh informing them of the Prophet's ﷺ intention and sent it with a woman. Revelation informed the Prophet ﷺ, and he sent men who intercepted her and took the letter. When the Prophet ﷺ confronted Hatib he did not rush to judge him, but asked: “What made you do this?” Hatib admitted it and gave his reason: he did it out of fear for his family and property in Makkah, not out of disbelief or apostasy. ‘Umar wanted to kill him as a traitor, but the Prophet ﷺ stopped him, saying: “He fought at Badr, and how do you know? Perhaps Allah looked at the people of Badr and said: Do as you wish, for I have forgiven you.”
hatib-baltaa.historicalContext: This happened just before the conquest of Makkah in the eighth year after the migration, and verses of Surah al-Mumtahanah were revealed about it.
hatib-baltaa.problemType: Discovering what looks like outright betrayal by someone who was trusted and has a long record of loyalty
hatib-baltaa.responseType: Confronting directly with a calm question before judging, listening to the excuse, and weighing the seriousness of the act against the person's record
emotionsAddressed: Shock at betrayal by someone close
The urge to cut off or punish immediately
Doubting the intentions of the one who erred
principles: Calm confrontation and a direct question are a necessary step before passing any judgement
The motives behind an act may soften the judgement without cancelling the wrongness of the act itself
A person's long record of loyalty has weight when assessing an incidental mistake, even a big one
The harshest possible reaction is not always the right one
modernApplications: Before cutting off someone you discovered doing something that looks like betrayal, ask them directly and calmly about their motives
Distinguish between the seriousness of what happened and the intention behind it; the motive may not be what you imagine
Weigh the current situation in light of the whole history of the relationship, not this moment alone
Do not let your first angry reaction, or that of those around you, decide the fate of the relationship
notToApplyTo: This does not mean tolerating repeated or deliberate betrayals with no real excuse
This situation occurred in a very particular context and is not a general rule for dropping consequences in every betrayal
behaviorObservations: He did not pass judgement before confronting Hatib directly and asking him
He listened to his whole explanation before any reaction
He stopped ‘Umar from carrying out the harshest possible punishment, though the act was truly serious
He weighed the seriousness of the act against Hatib's record of loyalty
whatToAvoid: Judging someone's intention without asking them directly
Ignoring the entire history of a relationship because of one mistake, even a grave one
hatib-baltaa.reflection: Verifying before judging does not mean justifying every mistake; it means giving the truth enough of a chance to appear before final decisions are made.
keywords: someone close to me betrayed my trust
i discovered betrayal by someone i trust
my friend stabbed me in the back

quranRefs.context: Revealed about Hatib ibn Abi Balta‘ah when he sent a letter to Quraysh warning them of the Prophet's ﷺ plan to march on them
quranRefs.relevance: It shows how serious it is to leak secrets to opponents, and came in a context where the Prophet ﷺ accepted Hatib's excuse and did not exclude him from faith

hadithRefs.narrator: ‘Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him)

contrasts: In the first he asked about the motive and forgave; in the second he rejected assuming one knows the motive without asking — both reject hasty judgement from different angles

wafat-ibrahim.title: The death of Ibrahim: when grief and acceptance meet
participants: ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf (may Allah be pleased with him)
wafat-ibrahim.eventDescription: When his son Ibrahim's illness grew severe and he was in his final moments, the Prophet ﷺ came in and his eyes began to shed tears. ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf was surprised at his weeping, and he answered: “O Ibn ‘Awf, it is mercy.” Then he said: “The eye weeps and the heart grieves, but we say only what pleases our Lord. And we are saddened by your departure, O Ibrahim.”
wafat-ibrahim.historicalContext: Ibrahim, the Prophet's ﷺ son, died as an infant. A solar eclipse happened on the day of his death and some people thought it was because of his death, so the Prophet ﷺ later corrected this understanding.
wafat-ibrahim.problemType: Losing a loved one and dealing with the natural grief that comes with it
wafat-ibrahim.responseType: Not hiding grief, while combining it with acceptance and submission to Allah
emotionsAddressed: Grief over loss
Feeling guilty for crying
Confusing grief with resentment
principles: Grief and tears do not contradict patience and acceptance of Allah's decree
Honest expression of feelings does not reduce faith or trust in Allah
One can feel the loss while refraining from resenting the decree
modernApplications: Do not feel guilty if you cry over losing a loved one; it does not contradict faith or patience
Separate healthy expression of grief from resentment or objecting to the decree
Give yourself and those around you space for natural grief without suppressing feelings
notToApplyTo: This does not justify wailing or explicitly objecting to Allah's decree; the difference between natural grief and resentment is subtle but important
behaviorObservations: He did not stop himself from weeping despite his standing
He explained the difference between natural mercy and resentment of the decree
He combined “we are saddened” with “we say only what pleases our Lord” in the same sentence
whatToAvoid: Thinking that showing grief is a kind of weak certainty
wafat-ibrahim.reflection: This situation shows a beautiful reconciliation between the heart that grieves and the tongue that speaks only what pleases Allah.
keywords: deep grief after a relative died
a relative died and i'm very sad

quranRefs.context: A Quranic foundation for the meaning of being tested by the loss of lives (including children), and that patience in it is given glad tidings, not blamed
quranRefs.relevance: It places Ibrahim's loss within the general law of trial for which Allah promised the patient glad tidings

hadithRefs.narrator: Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him)

mihnat-ahlih.title: Serving his family: the example inside the home
mihnat-ahlih.eventDescription: ‘A'ishah was asked: What did the Prophet ﷺ do in his house? She answered: “He used to mend his clothes, repair his sandals, and do what men do in their homes.” In another narration: “He was a human being like others: he would check his garment, milk his sheep and serve himself.”
mihnat-ahlih.historicalContext: These narrations describe the Prophet's ﷺ daily life at home, away from his public duties as prophet and leader.
mihnat-ahlih.problemType: Sharing household tasks, cooperation and understanding within the family
mihnat-ahlih.responseType: Actually taking part in household work without seeing it as beneath his standing
emotionsAddressed: Feeling the household load is unbalanced
Tension from disagreements in shared daily life
principles: Taking part in housework does not contradict any social or religious standing, however high
The true example shows in private household details, not only in public appearance
Serving one's family and sharing daily tasks is a virtue, not a flaw
modernApplications: Do not consider helping with daily housework as lowering your standing
Balance household tasks based on ability and time, not only on rigid traditional roles
Bring the same spirit of humility and cooperation when a disagreement arises with your spouse; daily cooperation is a solid foundation before any dispute
notToApplyTo: This text should not be used to impose a fixed, rigid division of tasks; the point is the principle of sharing, not the details
behaviorObservations: He served himself despite the demands of his mission and leadership
He did not consider serving himself or helping at home something exceptional worth mentioning, except when asked
whatToAvoid: Using this text to impose a fixed division of tasks on the other person
mihnat-ahlih.reflection: The true example is often in the details people do not see, not in public moments.

is it right for a man to do housework

kaab-ibn-malik.title: The three who stayed behind: firmness with honesty, not with every excuse
participants: Ka‘b ibn Malik and his two companions (may Allah be pleased with them)
kaab-ibn-malik.eventDescription: Ka‘b ibn Malik and two companions stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk without a valid excuse. When the Prophet ﷺ returned and asked them for their excuse, Ka‘b told the truth and said he had no real excuse, although he could have invented one that would have been accepted. The Prophet ﷺ said: “As for this one, he has told the truth. Get up until Allah decides about you.” Then the Prophet ﷺ ordered a social boycott of the three for fifty nights, until their repentance was revealed in the Quran.
kaab-ibn-malik.historicalContext: This happened after the expedition of Tabuk in the ninth year after the migration; it is a famous story that Ka‘b himself narrates in detail in al-Bukhari and Muslim.
kaab-ibn-malik.problemType: Dealing with someone who fell short of a clear commitment and then told you the whole truth without dressing it up
kaab-ibn-malik.responseType: Distinguishing the one honest in his admission from others, and applying a clear consequence without shaming or humiliating
emotionsAddressed: Disappointment with someone who broke a promise or commitment
Being torn between punishing the one at fault and accepting their excuse
principles: Honesty in admitting a failing deserves different treatment from lying or justifying
Temporary firmness (like the boycott here) can be a means of growth, not vengeful punishment
Accepting sincere repentance later does not contradict imposing a clear consequence for the failing
modernApplications: If someone tells you honestly about their failing without false justification, treat their honesty differently from someone who lies to you
A temporary distance can be a more suitable means of growth than a final break or completely ignoring the failing
Keep the door open for return if real change appears after the period of accountability
notToApplyTo: This does not apply to someone who keeps failing without real change, or to deliberate betrayals with no honesty in them
behaviorObservations: He distinguished between the one honest in his admission and those who lied or made excuses
He did not shame them publicly, but limited himself to a social measure for a set period
He accepted their return once their repentance proved sincere, without continual reproach
whatToAvoid: Treating someone honest in their admission the same as someone who lies or evades responsibility
kaab-ibn-malik.reflection: Sometimes a temporary distance is kinder to a relationship in the long run than immediately overlooking a real failing.
keywords: someone failed their commitment then admitted it honestly
should i forgive someone who honestly admitted his mistake

quranRefs.context: Revealed accepting the repentance of Ka‘b ibn Malik and his two companions after the social boycott
quranRefs.relevance: It shows that temporary firmness can be a path to real repentance, not the end of the relationship

hadithRefs.narrator: Ka‘b ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him)

ghar-thawr.title: In the cave: steadfastness when fear is at its height
participants: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him)
ghar-thawr.eventDescription: During the Prophet's ﷺ migration from Makkah to Madinah, he and his companion Abu Bakr al-Siddiq hid in the cave of Thawr for three nights, escaping the idolaters of Quraysh who went out searching for them after offering a reward to whoever brought them back. When the idolaters came so close to the mouth of the cave that they could almost see them, Abu Bakr feared for the Prophet ﷺ, and the Prophet ﷺ reassured him: “Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us.”
ghar-thawr.historicalContext: This took place in the year of the migration and is one of the most dangerous moments in the Prophet's biography.
ghar-thawr.problemType: Intense fear or anxiety before a major event or imminent danger threatening failure or harm
ghar-thawr.responseType: Standing firm, reminding oneself that Allah is with us, and reassuring others while the danger continues
emotionsAddressed: Fear
Anxiety
Feeling helpless before a great danger
principles: Fear is a natural feeling, and steadfastness does not mean its absence but not giving in to it
Allah being with you is not a promise that danger will disappear, but that you are not alone in it
Reassuring those around you in moments of crisis is part of calm leadership
modernApplications: If you face a terrifying situation or a decisive choice, allow yourself to feel fear without letting it paralyse you
Remind yourself that feeling in danger does not mean you are alone in it
If those around you are more afraid than you, reassuring them may be your role in that moment
notToApplyTo: This does not mean abandoning precautions and means; the Prophet ﷺ took every possible means (hiding, a guide, covering their tracks) before relying on Allah
behaviorObservations: He did not deny the danger, but reminded of Allah's presence despite it
He stayed calm at a moment when the enemy was extremely close
He reassured his frightened companion without belittling his feelings
whatToAvoid: Thinking that faith means never feeling fear at all
ghar-thawr.reflection: True steadfastness is not the absence of fear, but stepping forward while you feel it.
keywords: afraid of the result of a decision i made
very anxious before an exam or interview

quranRefs.context: Revealed describing the migration and the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr hiding in the cave
quranRefs.relevance: It describes that very moment and affirms that Allah was with them and sent down tranquillity despite the evident danger

contrasts: Here: steadfastness before an expected danger, prepared for by hiding; there: submission to Allah's command before a pain that has already happened — two different tests of steadfastness
There: a sudden danger at the weakest moment (sleeping alone); here: a danger anticipated and prepared for — and in both, the same steadfastness

istikhara.title: Istikharah: learning to trust Allah when unsure
subCategories: Trusting Allah while taking the means
participants: Jabir ibn ‘Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with him), the narrator
istikhara.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ used to teach his Companions the istikharah prayer for all their affairs, big and small, as he taught them a surah of the Quran. He would say: When one of you intends a matter, let him pray two units of voluntary prayer, then make the istikharah supplication, asking Allah to choose for him what is best in his religion, his worldly life and his Hereafter, and to turn away from him what is bad for him.
istikhara.historicalContext: One of the hadith showing the Prophet's ﷺ educational method in teaching his Companions a practical way to deal with indecision.
prophetTraits: Trusting Allah while taking the means
istikhara.problemType: Being torn between several options and not knowing which is right
istikhara.responseType: Teaching a practical method combining supplication and action instead of passive waiting or a random decision
emotionsAddressed: Indecision
Anxiety about making the wrong decision
Feeling unable to predict the results
principles: Asking Allah's help in a decision does not replace thinking and taking the means; it completes it
Istikharah is a habit for all matters, not only big ones
Being content with what becomes easy after istikharah is part of trusting that Allah chooses well
modernApplications: When torn between two options, combine practical thinking (consulting, weighing pros and cons) with asking for help as fits your conviction
Do not wait for a supernatural sign after istikharah or consultation; go ahead with the option you favour, then be at peace with what becomes easy
Make asking for help a regular habit in your small decisions, not only big ones
notToApplyTo: Istikharah does not replace gathering information and practical consultation before deciding
behaviorObservations: He made istikharah a regular habit in all matters, not an exceptional act
He linked supplication to a concrete action (two units of prayer), not to wishing alone
He taught his Companions a practical formula they could repeat themselves
whatToAvoid: Waiting for a decisive feeling or sign after istikharah instead of going ahead with the preferred decision
istikhara.reflection: Teaching istikharah beautifully combines trust in Allah with serious effort to find what is right.
keywords: i don't know which decision is right
how to make the right decision
i don't know what to choose

neighbors.title: The neighbour's right: advice repeated until it seemed he would inherit
participants: ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar (may Allah be pleased with them)
neighbors.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ told his Companions that Jibril kept advising him about the neighbour's right, again and again, until the Prophet ﷺ thought from the sheer amount of this advice that Allah would give the neighbour a share in his neighbour's inheritance.
neighbors.historicalContext: One of the comprehensive hadith highlighting the standing of the neighbour's right in Islam, regardless of the neighbour's religion or kinship.
neighbors.problemType: Dealing with neighbours, or a dispute or tension with someone who shares your space
neighbors.responseType: Raising the neighbour's right to the point of treating them almost as a family member
emotionsAddressed: Tension from a dispute with a neighbour
Feeling that neighbours' rights are a secondary matter
principles: The neighbour's right in Islam ranks very high, close to the rights of kinship
Repeated advice from revelation shows that good neighbourliness is not a detail but a moral foundation
The neighbour's right does not require them to be Muslim or a relative
modernApplications: Treat your neighbours by a standard closer to family than strangers
If a dispute arises with a neighbour, remember that living next to each other every day is a long-term relationship worth extra effort
Start with small, repeated kindnesses; they are what actually build good neighbourliness
behaviorObservations: He conveyed Jibril's advice faithfully without playing it down
He described how often it was repeated in a way that showed the Companions how much revelation cared about this right
whatToAvoid: Belittling neighbours' rights as a minor social detail
neighbors.reflection: When divine guidance about something is repeated, it is a sign that it is deeper than it first appears.
keywords: how to deal with an annoying neighbor

hadithRefs.narrator: ‘A'ishah and ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar (may Allah be pleased with them)

sighar-kibar.title: Mercy to the young, respect for the old: an inseparable balance
sighar-kibar.eventDescription: The Prophet ﷺ made combining mercy to the young and respect for the old a sign of belonging to his way, saying: “He is not one of us who does not show mercy to our young and respect to our elders,” joining gentleness towards those weak in age with respect for those who came before in age or experience.
sighar-kibar.historicalContext: A comprehensive hadith among the general educational hadith on social conduct.
sighar-kibar.problemType: Dealing with age groups whose rights may be overlooked or whose sensitivities may be forgotten
sighar-kibar.responseType: Linking belonging to the Prophet's ﷺ way with combining mercy to the young and respect for the old
emotionsAddressed: Running out of patience with children
Dismissing or ignoring the views of the elderly
principles: Mercy to the young and respect for the old are complementary values; neither replaces the other
The measure of good character includes how you treat those with no power over you and those past their visible prime
This balance is an honest test of character away from social courtesy
modernApplications: Watch how you treat the children around you when no one is watching
Give the elderly in your life real time and attention, not seasonal courtesy
Make mercy and respect a daily habit, not an occasion
behaviorObservations: He combined two complementary values in one concise sentence
He made the absence of either a deficiency in belonging to his way
whatToAvoid: Believing that respect means following an elder's opinion completely without thinking
sighar-kibar.reflection: When mercy to the weak and respect for the old meet in one character, a balanced moral scale is complete.
